blocks.text: Glory be to him who created the peacock, a bird of exceptional beauty, which in the variety of its colours resembles a bride. Scales are set into its feathers. In its dwelling many suns rise. On its crown a little tree ^{a)} is planted. It struts in pomp as though in a violet garment. In Arabic, as though in a violet. But there violet is taken for a garment of violet, or purple colour, which stands out most among the other colours in the neck and tail of the peacock. Hence Tertullian above: Deeper than any purple dye, where the neck blooms. And Achilles Tatius, book 1: Ὁ δὲ τοῦ ταῶ λειμὼν εὐανθέστερος· πεφύτευται γὰρ αὐτῷ καὶ χρυσὸς ἐν τοῖς πτεροῖς, κύκλῳ δὲ τὸ ἁλουργὲς τὸν χρυσὸν περιθέει τὸν ἴσον κύκλον [Ho de tou taō leimōn euanthesteros; pephyteutai gar autō kai chrysos en tois pterois, kyklō de to halourges ton chryson peritheei ton ison kyklon]. The meadow of the peacock (than any meadow) is more flowery: for in its feathers gold also is set, and purple surrounds the gold in an equal circle. To this belongs the description of the peacock by Publilius Syrus:

As though Babylonian were the same as purple, since Arrian in the Periplus mentions purple from Apologus, a city of Babylonia, at the mouth of the Euphrates. And Philostratus, Epistle 28, to a woman, praises τὸν Βαβυλώνιον κόκκον [ton Babylōnion kokkon]. Accordingly, אדרת שנער, the mantle of Shinar, or Babylonian mantle, Ios. VII, 21, is for Rabbi Chanina a mantle מן פרפרא בבלאה, of Babylonian purple; and for Jerome scarlet. But by feathered Babylonian we understand variegated. For, as we have proved elsewhere from Pliny and others, to weave different colours into a picture Babylon most made famous and gave it its name. We are led to this by these words of Aelian on the peacock, book 5, ch. 21: Δεικνὺς φιλοπόνως τὸ τῆς πτερώσεως πολύμορφον ὑπὲρ τὴν τῶν Μήδων ἐσθῆτα, καὶ τὰ τῶν Περσῶν ποικίλματα [Deiknys philoponōs to tēs pterōseōs polymorphon hyper tēn tōn Mēdōn esthēta, kai ta tōn Persōn poikilmata]; Ostentatiously displaying the multiform appearance of its plumage, surpassing the garment of the Medes and the varied colours of the Persians. Accordingly Antiphon, in his speech On the Peacocks against Erasistratus, cited by Athenaeus, book 9, and by Aelian in the place above, nowhere calls peacocks by their proper name, that is, ταῶνας [taōnas], but only ὄρνεις ποικίλους [orneis poikilous], variegated birds; as if by this very feature they were most distinguished from others.

[II, 713] From this same speech, compared with the life of Pericles in Plutarch, it is gathered [col. 139] that around the time of Pericles peacocks began to be kept at Athens in the house of a certain Demus, son of Pyrilampes, who made great profit from it. For he exhibited them to be viewed for a fixed fee at every new moon. And to this spectacle the curious flocked from Lacedaemon and Thessaly, that is, from both extremities of Greece. He also sold a male and female of the peacock kind for a thousand drachmas. Indeed, in Greece peacocks were not yet common in the age of Alexander, who, on the testimony of Aelian, ἐν Ἰνδοῖς ἰδὼν τοὺς δὲ τοὺς ὄρνιθας ἐξεπλάγη, καὶ τοῦ κάλλους θαυμάσας, ἠπείλησε τῷ καταθύσαντι ταὼν ἀπειλὰς βαρυτάτας [en Indois idōn tous de tous ornithas exeplagē, kai tou kallous thaumasas, ēpeilēse tō katathysanti taōn apeilas barytatas], seeing those birds among the Indians was astonished, and, admiring their beauty, fixed a heavy penalty for those who should kill them. Likewise at Rome Hortensius, as the same author reports, καταθύσας ἐπὶ δείπνῳ ταὼν πρῶτος, ἐκρίθη [katathysas epi deipnō taōn prōtos, ekrithē], having been the first to slaughter a peacock for a dinner, was summoned to court: or, as others read, κατεκρίθη [katekrithē], was condemned, or fined. Yet, as luxury prevailed, many following Hortensius raised the prices of peacocks; so much so that in Varro Merula asserts that in his time their eggs sold for five denarii each, the birds themselves easily for fifty. And that M. Aufidius Lurco made an annual income of over sixty thousand sesterces from flocks of peacocks. For although the flesh of the peacock tastes no better than the flesh of a hen, the peacock was valued much more highly because of its tail and feathers: as if this concerned the palate, or as if they ate the feathers with the flesh. This folly of gluttons Horace wittily mocks in these words, book 2, Satire 2:

Yet I shall hardly keep you, when a peacock is served, from wishing to wipe your palate with it rather than with a hen, corrupted as you are by empty things: because the rare bird is sold for gold and spreads a spectacle with its painted tail. As if that mattered at all. Do you eat that plumage you praise? Once it is cooked, does the same glory remain? Yet though in flesh there is no difference, it is plain that you are deceived by the unequal appearance into preferring this to that. — —

For these dishes were valued not for their flavour but for their price; nor were they sought for any other reason than that they sold more dearly, like parrots brought from India. Claudian, Against Eutropius, book 2:
Who whet the belly with price, and hand over to the palate the starry birds of Juno, and any green bird skilled in speech brought from the coloured Indians.

What of the fact that in Symeon Seth the flesh of the peacock is ἰνώδης, καὶ περιττωματικὴ, καὶ δύσπεπτος, καὶ κακόχυμος [inōdēs, kai perittōmatikē, kai dyspeptos, kai kakochymos], fibrous, productive of excrements, hard to digest, and of bad juice? Just as in Galen it is σκληροτέρα, καὶ δυσπεπτοτέρα, καὶ ἰνωδεστέρα [sklērotera, kai dyspeptotera, kai inōdestera].
